key_terms.meaning: The frequency f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)) at which X_L = X_C, so Z = R and the current is maximum
f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)) in hertz, where L is in henry and C in farad; ω₀ = 1/√(LC) in rad/s
The two frequencies f₁ and f₂ where the current falls to 1/√2 of its resonant value, so power is halved
At series resonance V_L = V_C = Q × V_s, so the coil and capacitor voltages can far exceed the supply
The frequency where the susceptances of L and C cancel, so the tank presents maximum impedance and the supply current is minimum
The resistance R_d = L/(CR) that a practical parallel tank shows at resonance
Q = 2π × (peak energy stored)/(energy lost per cycle); for a series coil Q = ω₀L/R = 1/(ω₀CR)
BW = f₂ − f₁ = f₀/Q, the width in hertz between the half-power frequencies
The ability of a tuned circuit to accept the wanted band and reject neighbours; it rises as Q rises and bandwidth narrows
The frequency f_c = 1/(2πRC) where an RC low-pass gain falls to 1/√2 = 0.707 of its maximum, i.e. −3 dB
A plot of gain magnitude and phase angle against frequency, usually on a log frequency axis
L = NΦ/I in henry: the flux linkage per ampere produced by the coil's own current
M = N₂Φ₁₂/I₁ in henry: the flux linkage in coil 2 caused by current in coil 1
k = M/√(L₁L₂), from 0 (no shared flux) to 1 (all flux shared, tight coupling)
A mark on each coil such that currents entering both dots produce aiding flux; it fixes the sign of the M term
a = N₂/N₁; an ideal transformer gives V₂/V₁ = a and I₂/I₁ = 1/a
A load Z_L on the secondary appears as Z_L/a² at the primary of an ideal transformer
MMF = NI in ampere-turns, the magnetic driving force set up by N turns carrying I ampere
R = l/(μA) in ampere-turns per weber (AT/Wb), the opposition of a magnetic path to flux
A small air gap adds a large reluctance because μ_air is about 1/1000 of μ_iron, which flattens the flux

takeaways: Series resonance happens when X_L = X_C, the impedance collapses to R, and the current peaks at f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)).
Parallel resonance is the dual: susceptances cancel, impedance peaks, and the supply current dips to a minimum.
Q = ω₀L/R ties together stored energy, bandwidth (BW = f₀/Q) and selectivity, so one number controls three ideas.
An RC circuit gives one first-order −3 dB corner, while an RLC circuit gives a band-pass peak whose sharpness is set by Q.
Self-inductance is a coil reacting to its own current; mutual inductance is the same flux reaching a second coil.
The coefficient of coupling k = M/√(L₁L₂) says how much of the flux is shared, from 0 to a maximum of 1.
The dot convention is a bookkeeping rule: it decides whether the mutual voltage adds (+M) or subtracts (−M) in the KVL equation.
An ideal transformer scales voltage by a, current by 1/a and impedance by a², with no loss; a linear transformer keeps finite magnetizing inductance.
Magnetic circuits follow Ohm's law in magnetic form: flux Φ = MMF/reluctance, with reluctance R = l/(μA).
bank_note: Long answers usually demand the impedance expression first, then the resonant condition, then the Q–bandwidth relation pushed through a numerical part; coupled-coil and transformer questions expect correct dot-convention KVL signs and the turns-ratio relations.

bank.q: Define series resonance. Starting from the impedance of a series RLC circuit, derive the resonant frequency and show that the current is maximum at resonance.
outline: At resonance Z = R, purely resistive
I = V/R is the maximum current, in phase with V

bank.q: Explain parallel resonance for an ideal tank and for a practical coil-capacitor tank. Define dynamic resistance and state the condition for maximum impedance.
outline: Ideal tank: infinite impedance, circulating current only
Supply current minimum, in phase with supply voltage

bank.q: Define the quality factor of a series RLC circuit in terms of stored energy and energy loss. Derive Q = (1/R)√(L/C) and relate it to bandwidth.
outline: Q = 2π × energy stored / energy lost per cycle
High Q means narrow band and sharp selectivity

bank.q: Explain self-inductance and mutual inductance. Define the coefficient of coupling and derive M = k√(L₁L₂).
outline: Flux shared is only part of total flux

bank.q: State the dot convention for magnetically coupled coils. Explain how it decides whether the coils are series-aiding or series-opposing, and give the equivalent inductance in each case.
outline: Dots mark terminals of like polarity
Currents entering both dots give aiding flux

bank.q: A series RLC circuit has R = 10 Ω, L = 100 mH and C = 10 μF, fed from a 20 V sinusoidal source. Find f₀, Q, bandwidth, the half-power frequencies, the current at resonance and the voltage across the capacitor at resonance.
outline: f₁ and f₂ from f₀ ± BW/2
V_C = Q × V = 200 V, showing magnification

bank.q: A coil of inductance 200 mH and resistance 20 Ω is connected in parallel with a 5 μF capacitor across a 50 Hz, 230 V supply. Determine the resonant frequency, the dynamic resistance and the supply current at resonance.
outline: Note R is not negligible, so use the practical formula
Supply current is minimum and in phase at resonance

bank.q: An RC low-pass filter has R = 1 kΩ and C = 100 nF. Find the cutoff frequency, the gain in dB at 1 kHz and at 10 kHz, and sketch the magnitude and phase response.
outline: Slope −20 dB per decade beyond cutoff

bank.q: Two coils with L₁ = 0.4 H and L₂ = 0.9 H are connected in series. The series-aiding inductance is 1.5 H and the series-opposing inductance is 0.9 H. Find M and the coefficient of coupling k.
outline: Subtract to get 4M, so M = 0.15 H

bank.q: An ideal transformer with 500 primary turns and 100 secondary turns feeds a 4 Ω load from a 230 V, 50 Hz supply. Find secondary voltage, secondary current, primary current and the impedance seen at the primary.

An iron ring of mean length 50 cm and cross-section 4 cm² carries a coil of 400 turns. The relative permeability is 1500 and there is a 1 mm air gap. For a flux of 0.5 mWb, find the reluctance of the iron, the reluctance of the gap and the coil current needed.
outline: Note that a 1 mm gap can dominate the total reluctance

bank.q: Compare series and parallel resonance in detail: impedance at resonance, current, the role of R, the meaning of Q, and the effect of Q on bandwidth and selectivity. Use a radio or TV tuner as the application.
outline: Series: Z minimum = R, current maximum
Parallel: Z maximum, supply current minimum
Circulating current is Q times supply current
High Q gives narrow BW, sharp selectivity, more ringing
Tuner selects one channel and rejects adjacent ones

bank.q: Two coupled coils are connected in a circuit with the dot on the first coil at the current entry terminal and the dot on the second coil at the far terminal. Write the KVL equations for both meshes and explain how the sign of the M term changes if one dot is reversed.
outline: Mutual voltage polarity from dot rule
Reducing dot to the other end flips the sign of M
Coupling coefficient unchanged, sign of M changes

bank.q: A receiver front-end tank must pass a 10 kHz channel and reject a station 20 kHz away. Discuss how the choice of Q trades off bandwidth against tuning sensitivity and component drift, and what limits the highest usable Q in practice.
outline: High Q narrows BW and improves rejection
Coil resistance and capacitor loss limit real Q
Temperature and component tolerance detune a high-Q tank
Sharp phase slope near resonance causes distortion
Practical compromise between selectivity and stability

bank.q: A magnetic circuit has a central limb carrying the coil and two outer limbs forming parallel paths. Explain, step by step, how you would find the flux in each limb using the electrical-analogy method.
outline: Reluctance of each limb from l/(μA)
Split flux between parallel limbs in inverse ratio of reluctance
Check by comparing MMF drops around each loop

glossary.def: The condition in a circuit containing L and C where the two reactances cancel and the circuit behaves purely resistively.
The frequency f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)) at which cancellation of reactances occurs.
The imaginary part of impedance: X_L = 2πfL for a coil and X_C = 1/(2πfC) for a capacitor, both in ohm.
The imaginary part of admittance, in siemens; parallel resonance occurs when the total susceptance is zero.
A frequency where the power delivered is half the resonant value, which means the current is 1/√2 of its peak.
The difference between the two half-power frequencies, equal to f₀/Q in hertz.
A dimensionless number comparing energy stored per cycle with energy lost per cycle; higher Q means a sharper, narrower response.
How well a tuned circuit separates the wanted frequency band from unwanted nearby frequencies.
The equivalent resistance L/(CR) that a practical parallel tank presents at resonance.
The frequency at which the gain of a first-order circuit drops to 0.707 of its maximum, a 3 dB fall.
A tenfold change in frequency; first-order filters change gain by 20 dB per decade beyond cutoff.
The phase shift between input and output at a given frequency, read from the phase plot of the frequency response.
The property of a coil that opposes change of its own current by inducing a voltage proportional to di/dt.
The property by which a changing current in one coil induces a voltage in a second coil linked by common flux.
The product NΦ, the total flux threading all turns of a coil, measured in weber-turns.
The fraction k = M/√(L₁L₂) of the total flux of one coil that links the other; it lies between 0 and 1.
A pair of marks on coupled coils such that currents entering both dots create flux in the same direction.
A connection where the two coupled coils carry current into the dotted terminals, giving L_eq = L₁ + L₂ + 2M.
A connection where one coil is reversed so its flux opposes the other, giving L_eq = L₁ + L₂ − 2M.
A lossless transformer with infinite magnetizing inductance and unity coupling, giving exact turns-ratio scaling of voltage and current.
A coupled-coil model with finite self and mutual inductances, analysed by mesh equations; it is linear but not ideal.
The driving force of a magnetic circuit, MMF = NI, measured in ampere-turns.
The opposition a magnetic path offers to flux, R = l/(μA), in ampere-turns per weber.
The property μ = μ₀μ_r of a material showing how easily it carries magnetic flux, in henry per metre.
A short non-magnetic length in a magnetic core; it has high reluctance and stores most of the magnetic energy.
